label: Title
notes: Open by framing the chapter as two local-to-global machines. Compactness turns infinitely many local open decisions into finite control, while connectedness turns local adjacency and path information into one-piece structure. Point students to the notebook and the printed page span before using the proof-dependency motif.

label: Open Covers
notes: Use the interval picture as the operational definition of compactness. The cover is allowed to be large or redundant; compactness asks whether finitely many named opens still cover everything. The grid check is not a proof, but it makes the finite subcover claim inspectable before the theorem formalizes it.

label: Compactness and Heine-Borel
notes: State compactness first in topological language, then specialize to the Heine-Borel theorem. The important contrast is that compactness mentions only open sets, while closed and bounded mentions Euclidean distance. The chapter proves that these descriptions coincide for Euclidean subsets.

label: Subdivision Proof
notes: Walk through the contradiction proof as a shrinking-witness argument. If no finite subcover exists, each subdivision keeps one bad square. Completeness forces the nested squares to converge to a single point, and openness around that point contradicts the square being bad at sufficiently small diameter.

label: Compactness Consequences
notes: Present these results as a toolkit rather than isolated facts. Compactness survives continuous images, passes to closed subsets, behaves well in Hausdorff spaces, forces accumulation for infinite subsets, gives extrema for real-valued functions, and supplies Lebesgue numbers for metric open covers.

label: Continuous Image Example
notes: The parabola example is deliberately simple because the theorem is doing the conceptual work. Compactness gives attained maximum and minimum values, connectedness prevents the image from breaking into separated pieces, and the symbolic derivative check verifies the displayed extrema exactly.

label: Product Topology
notes: Introduce product topology through rectangles because the product compactness proof uses exactly those basic opens. Emphasize the two projection facts: projections are continuous and open, and a map into a product is continuous precisely when its two coordinate projections are continuous.

label: Product Compactness
notes: Teach the proof as two rounds of finiteness. Compactness of the fiber chooses finitely many rectangles over one x. Their common x-overlap thickens the fiber to a strip. Compactness of the base then chooses finitely many strips, producing a finite rectangle subcover.

label: Closed Bounded Euclidean Sets
notes: This slide closes the compactness half of the chapter. Boundedness places the set inside a large finite product of compact intervals. Product compactness makes the box compact, and closed-subset compactness transfers that finite-cover property to the original Euclidean subset.

label: Connectedness Definition
notes: Define connectedness by what a successful separation would have to do. If X is the union of two nonempty pieces, the pieces must either meet or touch through closure. Then give the equivalent clopen and discrete-target tests, since later proofs often use those forms.

label: Connected Subsets of the Line
notes: Use the line theorem as the model proof. A connected subset of the real line cannot have a missing point between two of its points, because the missing point separates the subset into left and right pieces. Conversely, the supremum argument shows intervals have no such separation.

label: Stability of Connectedness
notes: This slide collects the methods for building connected spaces. Continuous images cannot tear a connected domain apart, dense closures inherit connectedness, unions of connected sets remain connected when their pieces are not separated, and products are connected by crossing through vertical and horizontal slices.

label: Components
notes: Components are maximal connected pieces, so every connected subset lives inside one of them. The finite sampled model of R minus two points shows three components, while the sine-curve model reminds students that components and path components can diverge sharply. This sets up the local connectedness warning on the next slide.

label: Paths
notes: Define paths as continuous maps from the unit interval and make concatenation explicit. Path connectedness is stronger than connectedness because a clopen separation would pull back to a forbidden clopen subset of the interval. Add the local hypothesis from the source span: in a locally path-connected space, connectedness is enough to recover paths, and open Euclidean subsets satisfy that condition. The sine curve warning shows what can fail without local path connectedness.

label: Topologist Sine Curve
notes: Use the topologist sine curve as the chapter's cautionary example. The oscillating graph is connected, its closure adds the vertical segment, and closure preserves connectedness. Yet no path can cross from the vertical segment into the oscillating graph, so path components split.

label: Recap Proof Map
notes: Close by reading the dependency graph from left to right. Open covers feed compactness, compactness powers products and Euclidean closed-bounded sets, connectedness travels through images and closures, and paths imply connectedness but not conversely. The checked node and edge counts keep the map accountable.
